docs.title: Mediterranean Travels
docs.text: A day-by-day travel guide for a November 2026 journey from Istanbul to Athens, exploring the history of civilization, culture, cuisine, and the people who live along the way.

docs.title: The Journey
docs.text:
Thirteen days through Turkey and Greece, November 11–23, 2026:

  • Nov 11–13: Istanbul on our own. Three days in the city that straddles Europe and Asia.
  • Nov 14–20: the Viking Star cruise. Ancient Mediterranean Treasures, from Istanbul past Troy and Ephesus to Rhodes, Crete, and Athens.
  • Nov 21–23: Athens on our own. Three days in the city where democracy, philosophy, and theater began.

The Trip Description has the full day-by-day itinerary, and the Viking Cruise Map shows the route port by port.

docs.title: How to Use This Guide
docs.text:
There is one chapter for each day of the trip. Read it at breakfast or the night before. Each chapter covers:

  • what we will see that day, and the stories behind it
  • details to notice that most visitors walk past
  • food and drink to try, and the history in the dish
  • the people who live there now, and how to be good guests
  • practical notes on timing, closures, and November weather

The Chapters page lists every day. Use the search bar to find a person, place, or dish.

docs.title: What's Inside
docs.text:
• Chapters: one per day, plus a chapter to read before we leave and one for the trip home.
  • MicroSims: interactive maps and other tools, starting with the cruise route.
  • Learning Graph: the map of ideas behind the guide. It lists the people, places, and events the chapters cover, and shows which ones help explain the others.

docs.title: About
docs.text: A day-by-day travel guide for a November 2026 journey from Istanbul to Athens, exploring the history of civilization, culture, cuisine, and the people who live along the way.

docs.title: Why This Guide Exists
docs.text: It is easy to visit Hagia Sophia, Ephesus, or the Acropolis, take a photograph, and move on. This guide exists to slow down and notice more. It is written for travelers who love the long history of civilization, who want to understand a culture through its food, and who want to meet the people of each place with real empathy, not just walk past them on the way to the next monument.

docs.title: Who It Is For
docs.text: The travelers on this trip: curious adults with no professional background in archaeology or classics. No prior knowledge is assumed beyond having heard of ancient Greece, Rome, Christianity, Islam, and the Ottoman Empire. Every other term is explained when it first appears.

docs.title: How to Use This Guide
docs.text:
• Read one chapter a day. Each chapter matches one day of the trip, from November 11 to November 23, 2026. Breakfast or the night before is the best time.
  • Read the before-you-go chapter first. It sets out the big timeline of the region and a few words of Turkish and Greek.
  • Use the Viking Cruise Map to see where each port is and how the ship gets there.
  • Search (top right) for any person, place, or dish.
  • Keep a journal. A few lines each evening about what we noticed, ate, and learned from the people we met is worth more than a hundred photographs.

Cruise port times come from cruise-agency listings and can change. Confirm them with Viking, and check opening hours locally, since November is off-season.

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Mediterranean Travels

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This is not a textbook. It is a personal travel guide for a thirteen-day journey through Turkey and Greece, from Wednesday, November 11 to Monday, November 23, 2026. The trip has three parts: three days on our own in Istanbul, the Viking Star's seven-night Ancient Mediterranean Treasures cruise from Istanbul to Athens, and three days on our own in Athens.

The guide is meant to be read one chapter per day, ideally at breakfast or the night before. Each chapter prepares us for that day's place: what happened there, who built it and why, what to look for when we are standing in front of it, what to eat, and who lives there now. The goal is not to tick off sights. It is to notice more, understand more, and meet the people of each place with real empathy.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: The travelers on this trip: curious adults who love the history of civilization, culture, and food, and who want to understand the people in each place, not just see the monuments. We have no professional background in archaeology, classics, or Middle Eastern or Balkan history.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: None. The guide assumes only general adult knowledge, such as having heard of ancient Greece, the Roman Empire, Christianity, Islam, and the Ottoman Empire. Every other term is explained when it first appears.

docs.title: Itinerary
docs.text:
Cruise port times are from the cruise-agency listings for the November 14, 2026 sailing (Cruisebound). Viking can change times and ports, so we should confirm with Viking before we go.

Day Date Place Plan 1 Wed Nov 11 Istanbul, Turkey Arrive; on our own 2 Thu Nov 12 Istanbul, Turkey On our own 3 Fri Nov 13 Istanbul, Turkey On our own; Friday is the main day of congregational prayer 4 Sat Nov 14 Istanbul, Turkey Embark the Viking Star (overnight in port) 5 Sun Nov 15 Istanbul, Turkey In port until 6:00 PM; the Grand Bazaar is closed on Sundays 6 Mon Nov 16 Çanakkale (Troy and Gallipoli), Turkey 9:00 AM – 4:00 PM 7 Tue Nov 17 Kusadasi (Ephesus), Turkey 7:00 AM – 6:00 PM 8 Wed Nov 18 Rhodes, Greece 7:00 AM – 6:00 PM 9 Thu Nov 19 Heraklion (Knossos), Crete, Greece 7:00 AM – 6:00 PM 10 Fri Nov 20 Athens (Piraeus), Greece Arrive 7:00 AM; final night aboard 11 Sat Nov 21 Athens, Greece Disembark; on our own 12 Sun Nov 22 Athens, Greece On our own 13 Mon Nov 23 Athens, Greece On our own

November is off-season. Opening hours are shorter, some sites close for the season, and it can be cool and rainy, so each chapter should flag what to check and what to wear.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• One chapter per day of the itinerary (thirteen chapters). Istanbul and Athens each get several chapters, so each day can focus on a different layer of the city instead of repeating an overview.
  • A short orientation chapter to read before departure: the big timeline of the region, a few words of Turkish and Greek, and how the trip fits together.
  • A short closing chapter to read on the way home: connecting what we saw across all the stops.

Every daily chapter should cover, where it fits:

  1. What we will see, in the order we are likely to see it.
  2. The history behind it, told as stories about people, not lists of dates.
  3. Things to notice that most visitors walk past.
  4. Food and drink to try that day, and the history in the dish.
  5. The people who live there now: daily life, work, faith, and what tourism means to them, especially in the off-season.
  6. Etiquette and a few useful words, so we can be good guests.
  7. Practical notes: timing, distances, closures, and weather.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
1. The long timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean, from the Minoans to modern Turkey and Greece
  2. Minoan Crete: Knossos, palace culture, and Europe's first civilization
  3. Troy, the Bronze Age, and how Homer's Iliad blends myth and history
  4. Classical Athens: democracy, philosophy, theater, and the Acropolis
  5. The Hellenistic and Roman worlds: Ephesus as a great Greco-Roman city
  6. Early Christianity in Anatolia and Greece: Paul at Ephesus, the House of the Virgin Mary, and the Orthodox Church
  7. Byzantium and Constantinople: Hagia Sophia, the cistern, and a Christian empire that lasted a thousand years
  8. The Crusades and the Knights Hospitaller of Rhodes
  9. Venice in the Eastern Mediterranean: the forts and harbors of Crete
  10. The Ottoman Empire: Topkapi Palace, the mosques, the bazaars, and a multi-faith empire
  11. The end of empires: Gallipoli, the birth of modern Turkey, Greek independence, and the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey
  12. Jewish communities of the region, including Rhodes' Jewish Quarter and the deportation of its community in 1944
  13. Islam in daily life: prayer times, mosque etiquette, and the call to prayer
  14. Turkish cuisine: breakfast, meze, kebab, simit, tea, coffee, and sweets
  15. Greek and Cretan cuisine: olive oil, bread, cheese, fish, wine, and the Cretan diet
  16. Daily life in Turkey and Greece today: families, work, the economy, faith, and attitudes toward visitors
  17. Being a thoughtful traveler: empathy, etiquette, a few words of Turkish and Greek, and seeing past the tourist script
  18. Reading a ruin: how to look at walls, columns, mosaics, and frescoes and understand what they tell us

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the trip, we will be able to:

  • Remember: name the main civilizations of the region in order, and the key site that represents each one on our route.
  • Understand: explain why each place mattered in its own time, and how empires, trade, and faith shaped its people.
  • Apply: use the daily chapter to plan each day around opening hours, port times, prayer times, and weather, and to order and enjoy local food with confidence.
  • Analyze: compare how Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Venetian, and Ottoman builders left their marks on the same places, and spot those layers on our own.
  • Evaluate: weigh competing stories about contested history, such as Troy, Gallipoli, Hagia Sophia, and the population exchange, and understand why Turks and Greeks may remember the same events differently.
  • Create: keep a short daily journal of what we noticed, ate, and learned from the people we met, and turn it into our own story of the journey.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
There is one chapter for each day of the trip, November 11–23, 2026, plus a chapter to read before we leave and one for the trip home. Read each day's chapter at breakfast or the night before.

Chapters are added by the book-chapter-generator skill once the learning graph is complete; their content is filled in by the chapter-content-generator skill.

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
The learning graph captures how concepts in Mediterranean Travels depend on each other. It is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — every concept has a path back to one or more foundational concepts that have no prerequisites.

Once the learning-graph-generator skill runs, this section will be populated with:

  • Course Description Assessment — quality review of course-description.md
  • Concept Enumeration — the ~200 concepts the guide will cover
  • Concept Taxonomy — concepts grouped into 8–12 categories
  • Graph Quality Analysis — DAG structure, foundational and terminal nodes
  • Taxonomy Distribution — concept count per taxonomy category

Use the book-installer skill (option 23) to add an interactive graph viewer once learning-graph.json exists.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small interactive tools, such as maps and timelines, that help us see where we are going and how the places fit together. Each one can also be embedded in a daily chapter.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

  • Viking Cruise Map - an interactive map of the Istanbul-to-Athens cruise with port times, key sights, and the sea route.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This map follows the Viking Star's seven-night Ancient Mediterranean Treasures voyage from Istanbul to Athens, November 14–21, 2026: the middle part of our November 11–23 trip. The cruise calls at six ports in Turkey and Greece:

  1. Istanbul, Turkey: Nov 14–15, overnight in port (trip days 4–5)
  2. Çanakkale, Turkey, the port for Troy and Gallipoli: Nov 16 (trip day 6)
  3. Kusadasi, Turkey, the port for Ephesus: Nov 17 (trip day 7)
  4. Rhodes, Greece: Nov 18 (trip day 8)
  5. Heraklion, Crete, Greece, the port for Knossos: Nov 19 (trip day 9)
  6. Athens (Piraeus), Greece: Nov 20, disembarking Nov 21 (trip days 10–11)

The map labels each stop by cruise day (Istanbul is cruise days 1–2). The daily chapters use trip days, which start with our own three days in Istanbul on November 11.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
• Step through the ports with the Next → and ← Previous buttons, the ← and → arrow keys, the numbered dots, or by clicking a numbered pin on the map. The map flies to each port as you select it.
  • Read the port card on the right. It shows the date, arrival and departure times, a short introduction, the key things to see, and a practical tip.
  • Follow the route. Legs already sailed are solid navy, the leg that brought you to the current port is gold, and legs still ahead are dashed blue.
  • Click Whole route to zoom back out to the full itinerary.
  • Switch base maps with the layer control in the top-right corner of the map: street map, satellite imagery, or OpenStreetMap.

The sea route is approximate. It shows the general track through the Dardanelles and around the islands, not the ship's exact navigation.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: This map is for us as travelers, not for a classroom. Here is how to get the most from it before and during the cruise.

docs.title: What We Will Get From It
docs.text:
• A clear picture of where each port is and which waters the ship sails through to reach it.
  • The one sight at each port that matters most, and the civilization that built it.
  • A realistic plan for each shore day that fits the port's arrival and departure times.

docs.title: Before We Leave
docs.text:
1. Route tour (5 minutes). Step through all six ports in order. At each one, notice the water the ship crosses to get there: the Sea of Marmara, the Dardanelles, the Aegean Sea, and the Sea of Crete.
  2. Choose at Çanakkale. Troy and Gallipoli lie in opposite directions, so decide in advance which story we most want to stand inside: the Bronze Age city of Homer's Iliad, or the 1915 battlefields that shaped modern Turkey, Australia, and New Zealand.
  3. Book early. Check which included excursion Viking offers at each port. The Ephesus and Knossos tours fill up first.

docs.title: Each Evening Aboard
docs.text:
1. Look ahead. Open the next port, read its card, then read that day's chapter.
  2. Plan the day. Using the arrival and departure times and the tip, sketch a schedule that gets us back to the ship at least 30 minutes before it sails.
  3. Look closer. Switch to the satellite map and zoom in on tomorrow's port. At Rhodes, find the walls of the medieval town; at Heraklion, find the Venetian fortress guarding the old harbor.

docs.title: Looking Back
docs.text:
• On the flight home, sketch the route from memory and label all six ports.
  • Put the main sight at each port in order of age, from Knossos (about 1900 BC) to Topkapi Palace (15th century AD), and note which empire built each one.
